newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak IRB's swing to loss raises analyst concerns.
newsitem.headline: Slovak IRB's swing to loss raises analyst concerns.

text.p: Investicna a Rozvojova Banka a.s. (IRB), Slovakia's third largest bank, swung to a loss in 1996 after heavy loan provisioning, but analysts said they were concerned about the bank's capital adequacy.

IRB said on Wednesday that it posted a 1996 loss of 1.2-1.3 billion crowns, after an after-tax profit of 167.5 million in 1995, while its capital adequacy ratio fell to 2.93 percent at the end of 1996 after 7.25 percent at the end of 1995.

Bank officials said the loss was due to IRB's heavier creation of reserves and provisions, securing its fast and successful restructuring. The ratio development was "in accordance" with the restructuring plan.
But analysts said the move was also questionable ahead of the bank's privatisation, expected sometime this year.

"One can work wonders with profits. I (as a bank) would prefer a loss to profit in the present situation to create provisions rather than pay taxes on profit," independent economist Juraj Rencko told Reuters.
Added a Slovak banker: "We could all manage this (bad loan portfolio) situation as quickly as IRB did. IRB figures now call for a capital injection".
In explaining the provisioning, IRB President Vojtech Vranay said the move was part of the bank's overall revitalisation plan, and would eventually strengthen it.
"Considering IRB's basic goal --to complete creation of reserves and provisions to cover potential risks-- shareholders sacrificed their profits, and the bank swung into a controlled loss," he said.

IRB officials added that their second basic goal was to strengthen the bank by boosting its basic capital through a share issue, in addition to a domestic subordinated debt issue to boost its overall capital.

"What IRB did is nothing unusual, even some Czech banks chose that (restructuring) way...if it's capital adequacy racio drop is within some agreeement with the central bank than it would be a step forward," one foreign banker said.

However, warned the Slovak banker, with the state privatisation agency the National Property Fund (NPF) suffering from a liquidity crisis and likely unable to participate in a basic capital increase, any such move would be a de facto privatisation of the bank.
"An IRB share issue means its privatisation, because its major shareholder -- the NPF is not likely to participate -- and VSZ would then take the whole bank," the banker said.

The state holds 35.14 percent in IRB through the NPF. Steel maker VSZ a.s. officially holds 14.6 percent of the bank and controls one-third of the seats on its supervisory board, but has tried to take control of the bank and often works in an alliance with other shareholders on major decisions.
The restructuring moves are the first visible signs of current IRB officials who took office two months ago after being appointed by the VSZ bloc.
Analysts have warned the presence of VSZ and allied companies as shareholders in IRB is a major risk for investors since VSZ is one the bank's biggest clients.
"More worrying than IRB's loss is the capital adequacy ratio, and the question of what happened to drag it down," Rencko added. The central bank requires bank capital adequacy ratio of 8.0 percent.

IRB's capital adequacy ratio drop has prompted some analysts to expectations of a central bank-forced reduction of the IRB's basic capital but the central bank declined immediate comment on IRB, adding they would be one of the topics on the agenda at Friday's NBS board meeting.

IRB officials said the restructuring project, based on creating reserves and provisions through "controlled losses", aims for the ratio to rebound to 6.5 this year, and to 8.07 percent by the end of 1998.
